items.title: The oil shock is a Brent shock: a $25 gap over WTI
items.subtitle: Brent (Europe) and WTI (Cushing, Okla.) crude oil spot prices, daily, dollars per barrel
items.take: Brent crude was $126.55 a barrel on October 14 and WTI was $101.91, a spread of $24.64. On October 8 the gap was $31.92, with Brent at $130.18 and WTI at $98.26, so the spread has narrowed by $7.28 in four trading sessions as WTI rose and Brent eased. Even after that narrowing, a premium of this size says the shock is concentrated in internationally traded, seaborne crude rather than U.S. inland supply. That matters for inflation abroad, where Brent-linked fuel costs bite hardest, and for U.S. refiners and exporters, which are buying crude far below the global benchmark.
items.source: U.S. Energy Information Administration via FRED (DCOILBRENTEU, DCOILWTICO)

items.title: Junk spreads are widening; investment grade is not
items.subtitle: ICE BofA US High Yield and US Corporate (IG) option-adjusted spreads, daily, %
items.take: The ICE BofA US High Yield option-adjusted spread stood at 3.16% on October 13, up 56 basis points from its 2026 low of 2.60% on August 28 and 33 basis points above its January 2 level of 2.83%. The investment-grade spread was 0.83%, only 4 basis points wider than on January 2. That divergence suggests investors are repricing risk in lower-rated, more energy- and consumer-sensitive borrowers rather than in credit broadly. With bank releases this week showing higher card-loss provisions, high-yield is the spread to watch for signs the oil shock is reaching corporate balance sheets.
items.source: ICE Data Indices via FRED (BAMLH0A0HYM2, BAMLC0A0CM)

items.title: From inverted to positive: the 2s10s Treasury curve
items.subtitle: 2-year and 10-year Treasury yields, daily, %
items.take: As of October 13, the 10-year Treasury yielded 5.21% and the 2-year 4.79%, a positive spread of 42 basis points on the Treasury's daily par curve. The chart shows how different that is from 2022 through 2024, when 2-year yields sat above 10-year yields for an extended stretch. A positive slope with both yields this high means lenders are demanding more to lend long, which feeds directly into mortgage, corporate, and federal borrowing costs.
